{"url": "https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.18126v1.pdf", "scope": "bounded PDF text extraction from up to 24 pages; figures, tables, equations, layout, and scanned-image text may be incomplete", "excerpt": "Fresh at Decision, Stale at Action: Routing New Information to LLM
Decisions Already Made
Ayoub Merimi and Souhail Bakkali and Abdeljalil Sakat
Abstract
Freshness shapes an LLM decision at the mo-
ment it is made; the action it commits to is la-
tent, carried out later, in a changing world. We
therefore introduce a timestamp theory of deci-
sion validity and a decision ledger that realises
it. Six timestamps define a decision; a fresh-
ness ceiling bounds what up-to-date evidence
guarantees at action time, placing the remain-
ing risk in information published afterwards.
Accuracy then factorises into two capabilities:
routing, which delivers that information to af-
fected decisions before their revision deadlines,
and temporal judgment, which reads it for the
time of action. The ledger is persistent state
holding each decision’s times, evidence and
background knowledge, indexed by watch con-
ditions written at decision time. Controlled
decision streams with exact labels confirm four
predictions across five LLMs, from 8B to fron-
tier scale: freshness alone yields exactly the
accuracy the ceiling predicts; models act on de-
cisive news once it arrives, so accuracy follows
routing; the ledger’s index sets what routing
reaches, and watch conditions reach indirect
dependencies at low exposure; and the remain-
ing errors concern when a change takes effect.
Freshness makes a decision right when it is
made; routing and temporal judgment keep it
right when it is carried out.

right at 13:05 and is wrong at 20:30. The informa-
tion that settles it appeared after the decision and

These lecture notes accompany the course "An Introduction to Judgment
Aggregation for Multi Agent Systems" given at the 18th European Agent
Systems Summer School.
/a.sc/b.sc/s.sc/t.sc/r.sc/a.sc/c.sc/t.sc
Reaching some form of consensus is often necessary for autonomous
agents that want to coordinate their actions or otherwise engage in
joint activities. One way to reach a consensus is by aggregating individ-
ual information, such as decisions, beliefs, preferences and constraints.
Judgment aggregation is a social choice method, which generalises vot-
ing, that studies the aggregation of individual judgments regarding the
truth-value of logically related propositions. As such, judgment aggre-
gation is applicable for consensus reaching problems in multi agent
systems. As other social choice theory, judgment aggregation research
is abundant with impossibility results. However, the aim of this tuto-
rial is to give an introduction to the methods of judgment aggregation,
not the impossibility results. In particular, the tutorial will introduce
the basic frameworks that model judgment aggregation problems and
give an overview of the judgment aggregation functions so far devel-
oped as well as their social theoretic and computational complexity
properties. The focus of the tutorial are consensus reaching problems
in multi agent systems that can be modelled as judgment aggregation
problems. The desirable properties of a judgment aggregation method
applied to these problems are not necessarily the same as properties
desirable in legal or political contexts, which is considered to be the
